summary.text: Direct finite minimality checks handle powers 9 and 27; for 81, the congruence of a decimal number modulo 81 in terms of its digit sum and a weighted digit sum, applied also to its reversal, forces any smaller common-divisibility candidate to have positive digit sum divisible by 81, contradicting that its digit sum is less than 81. For every larger exponent, start with a ten-digit block whose value and reversal are divisible by \(3^5\), repeatedly concatenate three copies (gaining a factor \(1+10^L+10^{2L}\), divisible by 3), and use its length \(10\cdot3^{n-5}<3^{n-2}\) to obtain a valid witness strictly below the all-nines number.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\operatorname{rev}(x)\) denote the integer obtained by reversing the decimal digits of \(x\), with any zeros that become leading zeros discarded. Thus, for example, \(\operatorname{rev}(270)=72\). For a positive integer \(q\), the definition of \(a(q)\) can equivalently be written
\[
a(q)=q\min\{k\geq 1:q\mid \operatorname{rev}(kq)\},
\]
provided the displayed set is nonempty. In all cases considered below it is nonempty because we exhibit a suitable \(k\).

We prove that, for every \(n\geq2\),
\[
a(3^n)=10^{3^{n-2}}-1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n\in\{2,3,4\}.
\]

First we establish the three exceptional values.

For \(9\), the least positive multiple is \(9\) itself, and its reversal is again \(9\). Hence
\[
a(9)=9.
\]

For \(27\), the number \(999=37\cdot27\) reverses to itself, so it is an admissible multiple. It remains to check that none of the positive multipliers \(k<37\) works. This is a small finite computation. For completeness, the residues modulo \(27\) of \(\operatorname{rev}(27k)\), listed in order, are
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrrr}
k&1&2&3&4&5&6&7&8&9\\ \hline
\operatorname{rev}(27k)\bmod27&18&18&18&18&18&18&9&18&18
\end{array}
\]
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrrr}
k&10&11&12&13&14&15&16&17&18\\ \hline
\operatorname{rev}(27k)\bmod27&18&9&18&18&9&18&18&9&9
\end{array}
\]
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrrr}
k&19&20&21&22&23&24&25&26&27\\ \hline
\operatorname{rev}(27k)\bmod27&18&18&9&9&18&9&9&18&9
\end{array}
\]
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrrr}
k&28&29&30&31&32&33&34&35&36\\ \hline
\operatorname{rev}(27k)\bmod27&9&9&18&9&9&9&9&9&9.
\end{array}
\]
Every residue is nonzero. Thus no \(k<37\) is admissible, and consequently
\[
a(27)=999.
\]

The value for \(81\) requires a general exclusion argument rather than a long search. We prove the following lemma.

**Lemma.** If \(0<x<999{,}999{,}999\), then \(x\) and \(\operatorname{rev}(x)\) cannot both be divisible by \(81\).

**Proof of the lemma.** Write the decimal digits of \(x\), from least significant to most significant, as
\[
L=(d_0,d_1,\ldots,d_{r-1}),
\qquad
x=\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}d_i10^i.
\]
Here \(0\leq d_i\leq9\), and because this is the ordinary digit expansion of a positive integer, \(d_{r-1}\neq0\). Put
\[
S=\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}d_i,
\qquad
W=\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}i d_i.
\]
Since \(10=1+9\), the binomial theorem gives
\[
10^i=(1+9)^i\equiv 1+9i\pmod{81};
\]
all terms involving \(9^2\) or a higher power vanish modulo \(81\). Therefore
\[
x\equiv S+9W\pmod{81}. \tag{1}
\]

For the reversed digit list, define
\[
W_R=\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}i d_{r-1-i}.
\]
The digit sum is still \(S\), so the same calculation yields
\[
\operatorname{rev}(x)\equiv S+9W_R\pmod{81}. \tag{2}
\]
This remains valid if the original units digit is zero: the reversal then has a leading zero, whose omission does not change its numerical value or any of the sums involved.

Reindexing the sum defining \(W_R\) gives
\[
W_R=\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}(r-1-i)d_i,
\]
and hence
\[
W+W_R=(r-1)S. \tag{3}
\]
If both \(x\) and its reversal are divisible by \(81\), equations (1) and (2), added together and then combined with (3), imply
\[
0\equiv 2S+9(W+W_R)
   =\bigl(2+9(r-1)\bigr)S\pmod{81}. \tag{4}
\]
The coefficient \(2+9(r-1)\) is congruent to \(2\pmod3\), so it is relatively prime to \(81=3^4\), and therefore is invertible modulo \(81\). It follows from (4) that
\[
S\equiv0\pmod{81}. \tag{5}
\]

On the other hand, \(x>0\) ensures that at least one digit is nonzero, so \(S>0\). Since \(x<999{,}999{,}999\), it has at most nine decimal digits. Therefore
\[
S\leq 9r\leq81.
\]
Equality \(S=81\) would force \(r=9\) and every one of the nine digits to equal \(9\), which would make \(x=999{,}999{,}999\), contrary to the strict inequality on \(x\). Thus
\[
0<S<81,
\]
which contradicts (5). This proves the lemma.

Now
\[
999{,}999{,}999=81\cdot12{,}345{,}679
\]
and this number is unchanged by reversal. It is therefore admissible for \(a(81)\). Every smaller positive multiple \(x\) of \(81\) lies in the range covered by the lemma, and hence its reversal is not divisible by \(81\). Consequently
\[
a(81)=999{,}999{,}999.
\]

These three values already establish the desired equality for \(n=2,3,4\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(3^2)&=a(9)=9=10^{3^0}-1,\\
a(3^3)&=a(27)=999=10^{3^1}-1,\\
a(3^4)&=a(81)=999{,}999{,}999=10^{3^2}-1.
\end{aligned}
\]

It remains to show that the equality fails for every \(n\geq5\). We do this by constructing, for each such \(n\), an admissible multiple much smaller than the number consisting of \(3^{n-2}\) nines.

Start with the ten-digit number
\[
V_0=4{,}899{,}999{,}987.
\]
Its reversal is
\[
V_0^R=7{,}899{,}999{,}984.
\]
Both are divisible by \(3^5=243\); explicitly,
\[
V_0=243\cdot20{,}164{,}609,
\qquad
V_0^R=243\cdot32{,}510{,}288. \tag{6}
\]

For \(m\geq0\), define \(V_m\) to be the decimal integer formed by repeating the ten-digit block \(4899999987\) exactly \(3^m\) times. Thus \(V_m\) has
\[
\ell_m=10\cdot3^m \tag{7}
\]
digits. Equivalently, \(V_{m+1}\) is obtained by concatenating three copies of the full decimal digit string for \(V_m\). Its reversal is obtained by concatenating three copies of the reversed digit string, because reversing three identical consecutive blocks again gives three identical reversed blocks.

We claim that
\[
3^{m+5}\mid V_m
\quad\text{and}\quad
3^{m+5}\mid\operatorname{rev}(V_m) \tag{8}
\]
for every \(m\geq0\). The base case \(m=0\) is exactly (6). For the induction step, suppose a decimal block represents an integer \(V_m\) and has length \(\ell_m\). Concatenating three copies gives
\[
V_{m+1}
 =V_m+10^{\ell_m}V_m+10^{2\ell_m}V_m
 =V_m\bigl(1+10^{\ell_m}+10^{2\ell_m}\bigr). \tag{9}
\]
Because \(10\equiv1\pmod3\),
\[
1+10^{\ell_m}+10^{2\ell_m}\equiv1+1+1\equiv0\pmod3. \tag{10}
\]
Thus (9) supplies one additional factor of \(3\). If \(3^{m+5}\mid V_m\), then \(3^{m+6}\mid V_{m+1}\). The identical concatenation formula applies to the reversed block, so the same reasoning gives \(3^{m+6}\mid\operatorname{rev}(V_{m+1})\). This completes the induction and proves (8).

Now fix \(n\geq5\) and set
\[
m=n-5.
\]
Then (8) says that both \(V_m\) and its reversal are divisible by
\[
3^{m+5}=3^n.
\]
Write \(V_m=k3^n\). Since \(V_m>0\), we have \(k\geq1\), and the divisibility of \(\operatorname{rev}(V_m)=\operatorname{rev}(k3^n)\) by \(3^n\) says precisely that this \(k\) is an admissible multiplier in the definition of \(a(3^n)\). Therefore
\[
a(3^n)\leq V_m. \tag{11}
\]

Because \(V_m\) has \(10\cdot3^m\) decimal digits, it satisfies
\[
V_m<10^{10\cdot3^m}. \tag{12}
\]
Meanwhile,
\[
3^{n-2}=3^{m+3}=27\cdot3^m>10\cdot3^m. \tag{13}
\]
Since powers of \(10\) are strictly increasing with their exponent, (13) implies
\[
10^{10\cdot3^m}<10^{3^{n-2}}.
\]
All quantities are integers, so this is equivalent to
\[
10^{10\cdot3^m}\leq10^{3^{n-2}}-1. \tag{14}
\]
Combining (11), (12), and (14), we obtain the strict inequality
\[
a(3^n)<10^{3^{n-2}}-1 \qquad(n\geq5). \tag{15}
\]
In particular, the proposed equality is impossible for every \(n\geq5\).

Finally, every integer \(n\geq2\) either is one of \(2,3,4\) or satisfies \(n\geq5\). In the first three cases the explicit evaluations above prove the equality, while in the latter case (15) disproves it. Hence, for all \(n\geq2\),
\[
\boxed{\ a(3^n)=10^{3^{n-2}}-1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n=2,\ 3,\text{ or }4.\ }
\]
